bible.title: The Great Emu War
bible.logline: In 1932, the Australian military faced off against a massive migration of emus destroying wheat crops in Western Australia.

places.name: Western Australia
places.visual_description: Vast, dry wheat fields and arid plains under a bright sun.

places.name: Campion
places.visual_description: A rural district characterized by dusty roads and agricultural land.

set_pieces.name: Lewis Machine Gun
set_pieces.visual_description: A vintage light machine gun used by the Australian military.

set_pieces.name: Wheat Field
set_pieces.visual_description: Golden wheat crops being trampled and flattened by large birds.

set_pieces.name: Barrier Fence
set_pieces.visual_description: A long, sturdy wire fence stretching across the landscape to block wildlife.

sentences: The Great Emu War
In 1932, the farmers of Western Australia were losing a war, and their enemy had feathers.
After the First World War, thousands of returning soldiers were given land to grow wheat.
Then the Great Depression hit, wheat prices collapsed, and a drought pushed about 20,000 emus inland, straight onto their farms.
The birds trampled crops and flattened fences, letting rabbits in behind them.
The farmers asked the government for help, and the government sent the army.
Major G. P. W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery arrived in the Campion district with two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns, and 10,000 rounds of ammunition.
The first attack came on November 2.
The soldiers spotted about fifty emus and opened fire.
The birds split into small groups and ran out of range.
Two days later, the soldiers set an ambush near a dam, where more than a thousand emus were gathering.
The gun jammed after killing only twelve.
Newspapers mocked the operation, and the army withdrew within a week.
Meredith returned in mid November and kept hunting until December 10.
By then his men had fired 9,860 rounds and claimed 986 kills.
That is about ten bullets for every bird.
Meredith was impressed by his opponent.
He said that if he had a division of soldiers with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds, it would face any army in the world.
In the end, the emus kept coming.
The government gave up on machine guns and paid farmers a bounty instead.
In six months of 1934, farmers claimed 57,034 bounties.
Today, Western Australia still uses long barrier fences to keep emus out of its wheat fields.

bible.title: The Great Molasses Flood
bible.logline: A massive steel tank bursts in 1919 Boston, sending a deadly wave of molasses through the streets.

cast.name: The Children
cast.role: Local residents caught in the wave

places.name: Boston
places.visual_description: A 1919 urban cityscape with brick buildings and cobblestone streets.

set_pieces.name: The Steel Tank
set_pieces.visual_description: A massive, cylindrical industrial steel tank painted dark brown, showing signs of structural weakness.

set_pieces.name: The Molasses Wave
set_pieces.visual_description: A towering, thick, dark brown wave of viscous syrup rushing through city streets.

set_pieces.name: Engineering Plans
set_pieces.visual_description: Blueprints and technical construction documents with official stamps and signatures.

sentences: The Great Molasses Flood
On January 15, 1919, in Boston's North End, a giant steel tank holding 2.3 million gallons of molasses burst open.
A wave of syrup up to 25 feet high rushed through the streets at 35 miles per hour.
It knocked buildings off their foundations and trapped horses, workers, and children.
Twenty-one people died and about 150 were injured.
Rescuers waded through waist-deep molasses for days, and the harbor stayed brown until summer.
Investigators found that the tank had been built in a hurry, never properly tested, and had leaked from the start.
The company had painted it brown to hide the leaks.
After the court case, Massachusetts began requiring engineers to sign off on construction plans.

bible.title: The Guest in Room 12
bible.logline: A night clerk at a Texas motel learns the touching reason behind a regular guest's annual visit to a specific room.

places.name: Amarillo
places.visual_description: A wide Texas landscape under a vast sky, featuring Route 66 and roadside motels.

set_pieces.name: Room 12
set_pieces.visual_description: A cozy motel room with fresh flowers on the nightstand, plush towels, and a warm glow from the heater.

set_pieces.name: The Night Desk
set_pieces.visual_description: A wooden motel reception desk with a crossword book, knitting needles, and a telephone.

set_pieces.name: The Envelope
set_pieces.visual_description: An envelope containing an old, faded photograph of a couple standing in front of a motel sign.

sentences: The guest in room 12
For six years, I worked the night desk at the Sundowner, a 40-room motel on Route 66 in Amarillo, Texas.
Nights were quiet.
I did crosswords, knitted scarves nobody asked for, and texted my wife to make sure she was still awake.
Every year on March 3rd, the same man checked in.
Mr. Alvarez was maybe seventy, with a pressed shirt and one small suitcase.
He always asked for room 12 and always paid $38 in cash, which was our price in the 1990s, and my manager Deb always let him.
One year, I finally asked him why room 12.
He smiled and said, "Because in 1974, it was the only room left, and she said yes anyway."
He and his wife had spent their honeymoon there.
She had died in 2016, and March 3rd was her birthday.
After that, I kept room 12 ready for him.
Fresh flowers from the grocery store, the good towels, the heater turned on an hour early.
He never mentioned it, but he always left a thank-you note on the pillow.
This March, he didn't come.
By midnight, I texted Deb: "Mr. Alvarez isn't here. Should I worry?"
She wrote back: "Keep the room. He's never missed one."
At 1:40 in the morning, a woman walked in holding a small suitcase I recognized.
She introduced herself as Sofia, his daughter.
Her father had passed away in January, and he had left her a list of things to do.
Number four was "Stay in room 12 on March 3rd and thank the night clerk."
She handed me an envelope.

Inside was a photo of her parents standing outside room 12 in 1974, the sign behind them exactly the same as it is today, and a note in his handwriting: "Thank you for keeping the heater on. She always said this place was warm."
Sofia stayed the night.
In the morning, she paid for room 12 for next March 3rd, and for the one after that.
She says she plans to come every year.
I don't work nights anymore.
Last fall, I bought the Sundowner from Deb.
Room 12 is never for rent on March 3rd.
